evidence.text: Xu Shen’s entry gives 龢 as “調也” and analyzes it as 从龠禾聲: 龠 is the semantic element and 禾 the sound element. This is a Han-dynasty lexicographic account, not by itself proof of the graph’s earliest origin. The dossier’s quoted 和 entry, “相譍也。从口禾聲,” was not independently located on the inspected Wikisource page.
evidence.title: 說文解字/03

evidence.source: Chinese Text Project dictionary entry, drawing on Guangyun, Kangxi, GSR and Hanyu Da Zidian
evidence.text: The entry for 龢 shows reported oracle-bone, bronze and seal forms and records the Guangyun statement that 和 is an old form. The site’s graphic display is evidence of a catalogued form sequence, but no glyph image was visually inspected here; it does not establish every proposed stage of change.
evidence.title: 龢 - Chinese Text Project

evidence.source: CUHK 21st Century journal article, “『和』的哲學——從中西冶金技術差異看中國文化”
evidence.text: The article reports old forms of 和 in bronze inscriptions and manuscripts, analyzes them as 口 semantic plus 禾 phonetic, and distinguishes 龢, analyzed as 龠 plus 禾. It proposes that 口禾 was an early form associated with taste adjustment, while 龢 related to musical tuning; these are the author’s interpretations, not a demonstrated single linear ancestry. The article gives no reproduced dated inscription in the inspected text sufficient to settle which form preceded the other.
evidence.title: 「和」的哲學——從中西冶金技術差異看中國文化

evidence.text: 禾 is listed with Mandarin hé and Middle Chinese hwa in Baxter’s transcription; the entry reports Old Chinese *[ɢ]ˤoj in Baxter–Sagart (2014) and *ɡoːl in Zhengzhang (2003). Those reconstructions place 禾 and 和 readings in a similar historical sound series. The source lists 禾 as pictographic for a grain stalk; this does not imply that the depicted grain’s meaning contributes to 和.
evidence.title: 禾 - Wiktionary

evidence.text: For 和, the entry gives Mandarin hé, Middle Chinese hwa, Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *[ɢ]ˤoj, and Zhengzhang *ɡoːl for the harmonious reading. It separately gives hè, Middle Chinese hwaH, Baxter–Sagart *[ɢ]ˤoj-s and Zhengzhang *ɡoːls for a musical-response/tuning reading. The page records a premodern citation from the Analects but does not date the first attestation of each individual sense.
evidence.title: 和 - Wiktionary

evidence.text: The Analects passage “禮之用，和為貴” attests 和 as a valued social or ritual quality, commonly rendered harmony. The text is traditionally associated with the pre-Qin period; this passage does not establish a precise composition or manuscript date, nor does it establish that this is the word’s earliest use.
evidence.title: 禮之用，和為貴 - Chinese Text Project

evidence.source: CUHK article, citing classical texts and later lexicography
evidence.text: The article separately illustrates harmony/state meanings, the verb ‘coordinate or adjust’ with citations to Zhouli, Guoyu and Shangshu, and ‘respond/follow’ with examples such as 一唱百和. It also discusses culinary adjustment and musical coordination. These examples show a broad semantic range, but the article’s list is not an ordered chronology; it does not demonstrate a dated chain from taste or sound to social harmony.
evidence.title: 「和」的哲學——從中西冶金技術差異看中國文化

evidence.source: Wiktionary, Chinese entry and historical-form display
evidence.text: The entry lists 咊 and 龢 as alternative forms and displays historical-form categories for 和 from Western Zhou, Warring States and Shuowen-era material. It characterizes 龢 as an earlier version in its analysis, while the CTP Guangyun record calls 和 an old form. This supports a reported historical relationship between the graphs, but does not securely establish that 龢 is the direct ancestor of every 和 form. 咊 is presented as an alternative graphic form, not established here as a chronological ancestor.
evidence.title: 和 - Wiktionary

gaps: The exact earliest attested graphic form and dating of 和 versus 龢 remain unsettled by the inspected material. Search-result claims that 龢 is the earliest and that 和 first appears in Warring States bronze need confirmation against primary inscription corpora and dated object records.
No visually inspected oracle-bone, bronze, manuscript or seal glyph was available in this research pass; graphic-development claims therefore rely on textual cataloguing and secondary descriptions.
The dossier’s Shuowen quote for 和 (“相譍也。从口禾聲”) was not independently verified in an accessible primary page. The accessible Shuowen text did verify the distinct 龢 entry (“調也。从龠禾聲”).

The proposed semantic role of 口 is not entirely uniform across accounts: the historical dictionary gloss for 和 emphasizes responding, while some secondary accounts propose mouth/speech, taste adjustment, or singing. Their exact origin interpretation remains disputed.

禾’s sound role in 和 is supported by component analysis and the shared reconstructed sound series. The source for the pictographic origin of 禾 does not establish that an original grain-stalk name motivated any borrowing; no whole-graph phonetic-loan claim is independently supported here.

No dated earliest attestations were established for each sense of 和, including harmony, adjustment, response, peace, and conjunction. Dictionary glosses and later example lists cannot supply that chronology.

The discussed Mandarin/Cantonese readings in the dossier were not comprehensively reverified. Historical phonological comparisons above are explicitly limited to the cited Middle Chinese and Old Chinese reconstruction systems; Japanese and Korean readings do not establish the graph’s origin.
